lesson.title: Chain Rule for Natural Logs: u Prime Over u
lesson.summary: Differentiating the natural log of an inside expression divides the inside function's derivative by the inside function itself, a pattern that later turns products and quotients inside a log into easy sums and differences.
lesson.body:
The derivative of the natural logarithm alone is d/dx[ln(x)] = 1/x. When the argument of the logarithm is a more complicated expression u instead of plain x, the chain rule formula gives d/dx[ln(u)] = (1/u) times u' = u'/u. This combines the derivative of ln x with the chain rule formula in the same outside-times-inside pattern used throughout this chapter, with the outside function f(t) = ln(t) contributing f'(t) = 1/t, mirroring how e^u worked with the exponential chain rule just before this topic.

The rule is simple to state but easy to misapply if the inside function is not correctly identified first, which is why recognizing composition matters here as much as anywhere else: ln(x^2 + 1) has inside function u = x^2+1, while (ln x)^2 is instead a power chain rule problem with ln(x) as the inside function of a squaring outside function. These two expressions look superficially similar but require different rules entirely, and confusing them is one of the more common mistakes once logarithms enter the mix.

Differentiate y = ln(x^2 + 1). Here u = x^2+1 and u' = 2x, so dy/dx = u'/u = 2x/(x^2+1). Check with Leibniz notation: let u = x^2+1, y = ln(u). dy/du = 1/u, du/dx = 2x, so dy/dx = (1/u)(2x) = 2x/(x^2+1), the same result. As a numerical spot check near x=1: y = ln(2), approximately 0.69315, and the derivative formula gives 2(1)/(1+1) = 1; comparing y at x=1.01, ln(2.0201) is approximately 0.70315, so the slope estimate is (0.70315-0.69315)/0.01 = 1.00, matching the predicted value of 1 closely. A second, simpler example: for y = ln(5x), u = 5x and u' = 5, so dy/dx = 5/(5x) = 1/x, which is a nice reminder that ln(5x) and ln(x) always differ by the constant ln 5, and constants vanish under differentiation.

Because the log chain rule divides by u, it is undefined wherever u is zero or negative, matching the domain restriction of the logarithm itself, so any derivative computed this way inherits the domain of the original function. This is worth flagging explicitly: ln(x^2+1) is defined for all real x since x^2+1 is always positive, so its derivative 2x/(x^2+1) is likewise defined everywhere, but a function like ln(x-3) would only be differentiable for x greater than 3, and asking for its derivative at x=2 would simply not make sense.

Logarithmic derivatives of this kind will later make it much easier to differentiate products and quotients raised inside a log, since ln turns multiplication into addition before you ever differentiate. That technique, called logarithmic differentiation, builds directly on this log chain rule and on the combining chain rule skills developed alongside product and quotient rules later in this chapter.

A last comparison worth making explicit: d/dx[ln(u)] = u'/u looks structurally different from every other chain rule in this chapter, since the outside function's derivative, 1/t, is a quotient rather than a power, an exponential, or a trig ratio. Students sometimes expect a copy of ln(u) to appear somewhere in the answer the way e^u appears in its own derivative, but ln disappears entirely once differentiated, leaving only the reciprocal of u times u' behind.
